title: AI for Regulatory Compliance in Banking: From SOX to Real-Time Monitoring
excerpt: . Financial institutions face expanding regulatory requirements , while many compliance processes remain manual. Tasks tied to frameworks such as the Sarbanes–Oxley Act (SOX) — including controls testing, documentation and audit preparation — are often handled through spreadsheets, disconnected systems and labor-intensive reviews, a model that is increasingly difficult for midsize banks to sustain. Artificial intelligence is beginning to change that. AI-enabled platforms can automate controls testing, generate audit-ready documentation and continuously analyze operational and transaction data to detect risk. For banks with between 500 and 5,000 employees, these tools offer a way to scale compliance operations without adding staff — shifting oversight from periodic manual reviews to continuous, data-driven monitoring. Click the banner below to learn how financial services are unlocking artificial intelligence’s potential. The Regulatory Compliance Challenge: Why Manual Processes Can't Scale. Manual compliance and processes rely heavily on spreadsheets, emails and human review, which make them slow and difficult to scale as regulations evolve. As the number of users, systems and access entitlements grows, organizations struggle to maintain consistent oversight and produce audit-ready evidence. “That’s the problem today — think how bad it’s poised to get with nonhuman identities (NHIs) and agentic services,” says Jim Taylor, RSA president and chief product and strategy officer. He says organizations increasingly need automated governance platforms to address this growing need, and maintain continuous visibility and control without relying on labor-intensive manual work. “They will need the speed and efficiency of automated solutions to keep up with NHIs and reduce their attack surface in real time,” he says. Sam Abadir, IDC research director for risk, financial crime and compliance, says AI can industrialize SOX operations by continuously assembling evidence from source systems, mapping artifacts to specific control requirements and identifying gaps before testing cycles begin. “The future SOX auditor works from risk signals across entire data sets rather than from static samples assembled for a point-in-time review,” he says. From his perspective, this evolution represents a shift from periodic control validation to continuous assurance based on full-population risk signals. Real-Time Compliance Monitoring: AI Tools for Risk Detection. Taylor explains that AI can continuously monitor regulatory publications, enforcement actions and supervisory updates, mapping changes directly to internal control inventories and policy frameworks to compress response cycles from months to days. “The advantage is not simply faster awareness of violations but earlier visibility into emerging risk conditions and control gaps,” he says. In Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) and sanctions programs, that ability to identify and remediate exposure before it surfaces in an examination is where the real value resides. title: RBI alert about AI-driven cyber risks, banks taking steps to plug vulnerabilities: Governor
excerpt: RBI alert about AI-driven cyber risks, banks taking steps to plug vulnerabilities: Governor. Synopsis. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra highlighted concerns regarding emerging cyber threats from artificial intelligence in banking systems. Measures are being implemented by banks and the RBI to secure IT infrastructure against these risks. The State Bank of India acknowledged potential data exposure, prompting increased vigilance for customer protection. Malhotra expressed confidence in India's robust forex reserves and external sector resilience amid these challenges. By PTI. Last Updated: Oct 23, 2026, 09:11:00 PM IST. Follow us. New Delhi: RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra on Friday said the central bank and other banks are alert about emerging cyber risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) agents and are taking measures to identify and plug vulnerabilities in their IT systems. title: Hong Kong regulator sets accountability, resilience, trust rules for bank AI
excerpt: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on Thursday announced the “Accountability, Resilience, and Trust (ART)” framework to promote the responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the banking sector as AI rapidly develops. Accountability is ensuring clear ownership, governance, and decision-making authority. Resilience focuses on secure, robust AI adoption that operates safely, fails safely, and recovers effectively. Trust is prioritizing fairness, transparency, explainability, and privacy. Under the framework, the HKMA issued the latest Supervisory Guidance for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence. The updated guidance focuses on three pillars: effective governance and accountability over AI adoption; proportionate management of the unique risks posed by AI; and building trust and transparency around AI solutions. title: Bank lays off 5,000 employees over AI.
excerpt: . Bank lays off 5,000 employees over AI. A bank has announced plans to lay off approximately 5,000 people, equivalent to 5% of its global workforce, thanks to improvements in work efficiency brought about by artificial intelligence (AI). VietNamNet • 24/10/2026. Barclays Bank (UK) has just announced a reduction of approximately 5,000 jobs as part of a cost-cutting initiative, which is being driven by advances in AI. This round of layoffs represents approximately 5% of the bank's total global workforce of 93,000 employees. Previously, management confirmed that they had cut 1,000 positions since the beginning of the year. Anna Cross, Barclays' Chief Financial Officer, said the plan is part of a strategy to save more than £1. 1 billion by 2027. "Around 60% of the cuts relate to support departments, including fewer programmers as AI helps make staff more productive," Cross said. You may also like. CS CEO Venkatakrishnan emphasized that the bank has invested heavily in technology and simplified operational processes. When asked about the direct impact of AI, he stated that streamlining processes is the main driver of current efficiency, while AI acts as the "icing on the cake" to modernize the system and will play an increasingly significant role in the future. Barclays' decision comes just months after Standard Chartered – another major UK-based bank – announced a plan to cut more than 7,000 jobs over the next four years due to increased AI adoption, and expects to shrink its back-office by around 15% by 2030. The layoff announcement came at the same time Barclays released its third-quarter financial results, with pre-tax profits reaching £2. 3 billion, up 12% from £2. 1 billion in the same period last year. Net profit from retail sales in the UK increased by 6%, reaching £2 billion, thanks to persistently high interest rates. You may also like. Meanwhile, the bank announced plans to return an additional £500 million to investors, bringing the total value of shareholder payouts through share buybacks and dividends since the beginning of the year to £2. 8 billion. This move immediately drew backlash from labor unions. Sharon Graham, General Secretary of the Unite union, criticized Barclays for "using AI as an excuse to eliminate loyal workers" and urged the bank to focus on upgrading employees' skills rather than implementing short-term solutions. title: AI poses moderate disruption risk to wealth managers and retail banks, Fitch says
excerpt: . AI poses moderate disruption risk to wealth managers and retail banks, Fitch says. Retail banks and private wealth firms scored 40 in Fitch's AI stress test, signaling possible one-notch downgrade risk under an adverse scenario. OCT 23, 2026. By Steve Randall. Artificial intelligence poses a moderate business disruption risk to financial institutions over the next five years, with wealth managers and retail banks among the most exposed, according to a Fitch Ratings report published October 22, 2026. Fitch assigned scores of 40 - on a scale of 0 to 100 - to retail banks, private banks and wealth management , and standalone wealth managers and advisory firms. A score of 40 signals the potential for a negative outlook and a possible one-notch downgrade for a typical issuer under an adverse scenario, Fitch said. For wealth managers specifically, Fitch identified elevated business model disruption risk as the primary concern. AI-enabled tools could automate or reduce the cost of investment advice, portfolio construction, research support, and advisory execution, the agency said. Fee pressure and commoditization of advice were cited as key threats, with Fitch noting that wealth management faces greater disruption than private banking, where high-touch client relationships are expected to remain intact and AI is more likely to augment than replace advisors. Retail banks' mass-market orientation leaves them vulnerable to AI-enabled fintechs and digital platforms competing on unsecured consumer lending, payments, deposits, and basic wealth advice, Fitch said. Loss of deposits could affect funding costs and ultimately profitability. Mitigants across financial institutions include regulatory barriers to entry, capital requirements, proprietary data, established client franchises, and the ability to build out in-house AI capabilities, according to Fitch. Corporate and investment banks scored 20, reflecting stronger protection from product complexity, bespoke human judgment, and high barriers to entry. All insurance sub-sectors also scored 20. Fitch said it does not anticipate AI driving sector-wide rating actions over the next five years, with fiduciary and regulatory obligations limiting full AI substitution in advice-driven businesses.
